mitigation_mechanism: The studies disagree. Most findings say agroforestry reduces drought losses, but the result splits by type of agroforestry, and several measured results show no benefit or harm, especially in severe or extreme drought. On the benefit side: in Isiolo County communities in Kenya, households rated agroforestry important during drought, farmers said deep-rooted trees reach water from deep down and keep producing fruit when there is no rain, and 74% of respondents had planted trees with drought in mind; the study concludes that agroforestry can and does build livelihood resilience to drought, citing deep root systems that use a greater soil volume for water [ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_t3_drought_deeproots_quandt17_7, ev_t3_drought_farmerquote_quandt17_12, ev_t3_drought_intentional_quandt17_14, ev_t3_drought_conclusion_quandt17_10, ev_t3_drought_roots_quandt17_2, ev_t3_drought_lh_quandt17_1]. Trees also share deep water: hydraulic redistribution in Sahelian parklands lets crop roots use deep soil moisture reached only by tree roots [ev_soil_water_retention_vannoordwijk21_3]. In a Senegal field trial, pearl millet grown among the native shrub Guiera senegalensis under an imposed in-season drought produced almost 10 times the biomass and over seven times more panicles than millet where the shrubs had been removed [ev_crop_yield_bogie18_1]. In an induced drought in eastern Canada only the monocrop lost yield, and the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Nyando District, Kenya, households in an agroforestry project typically used fewer detrimental coping strategies during hunger periods, and many farmers reported selling fuel wood and timber from their trees to buy food during the drought [ev_food_security_thorlak12_2, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. In a German alley-cropping system during a drought year, soil water content stayed lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system, though the differences were not significant at all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. In Sahelian parklands, trees make up a large share of high-quality livestock fodder, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, a practitioner article on the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system reports that, compared with farmers who remained with slash-and-burn, Quesungual farmers did not experience a total loss in maize production during the dry period of El Niño in 1997, which the authors put down to improved soil conditions [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2]. On paired on-farm plots in Ethiopia's Central Rift Valley, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns gave up to 85% more grain than open-field wheat in 2015, an El Niño year in which both yields were low [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. In Colombia, forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant in periods of intense drought while biomass in grass monoculture fell to 25% [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in 2009, the year with the lowest rainfall in several decades (440 mm), milk production still rose 10% on the previous year [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which reduces seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. Live fences of species such as Gliricidia sepium and Leucaena leucocephala supply livestock fodder in the dry season, when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. For shaded coffee and cocoa: in Ethiopia's Yayu coffee forest, the yield model for the climate-shock years found leguminous shade strongly raised coffee shrub yields at high canopy openness [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]; and reviews cite a 41% cut in evapotranspiration loss under coffee shade trees in the hot, dry season and low water stress in cacao grown with Gliricidia [ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_8, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11]. In a 25-year-old walnut-based alley-cropping system in southern France, winter pea still yielded less under the trees than in the full-sun control under both rainfall regimes, but the yield drop caused specifically by an imposed spring drought was smaller under the trees: full-sun yield fell 22% under drought while the alley-cropped yield rose by 12 to 20% relative to its own rainfed baseline, which the authors attribute to drought shifting yield formation from the shade-sensitive pod-set stage to grain filling [ev_crop_yield_blan22_2, ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3]. In a multi-site Argentine study of tree-covered pasture (silvopastoral systems) against treeless grassland, the normal-year forage benefit reversed under severe drought at some sites: at the semi-arid Santiago del Estero site the relative response swung from +2% in normal years to -89% in a dry year, while at the humid Chaco site it swung the other way, from -15% to +26%, and in the semi-arid aridity category overall there was no significant difference between systems in either normal or dry years — a result the authors attribute to tree-forage competition for water overtaking facilitation once drought intensity passes about 35% rainfall reduction [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_2, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_3, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_4, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_5, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_6].
caveats: The rating is conflicting because the types of agroforestry disagree: trees and shrubs regenerated on cropland show a strong reduction in drought losses, general findings not tied to one type show a small one, and planted tree-crop alleys, shaded tree crops and silvopasture each have studies on both sides. Few of the benefit findings say how large the effect is. The clearest harm finding is a direct field measurement in Ghana: during the extreme drought of 2015/16 all cocoa plants under Albizia ferruginea shade trees died and cocoa under Antiaris toxicaria suffered 77% mortality, while cocoa in full sun kept higher sap flux and soil water content was higher in full sun, pointing to competition for water between shade trees and cocoa [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. What separates the sides is mainly system and severity: deep-rooted trees in dryland fields and fodder trees in pastures read as buffers, while in shaded tree crops under extreme drought the trees compete with the crop for scarce soil water. Trade-offs pull the other way, now with more direct field evidence: in a semi-arid Kenyan growing season that received only 317 mm of rain, maize under dispersed Grevillea robusta trees yielded 0.02 t/ha against 1.53 t/ha in unshaded sole maize, a near-total loss under the trees in a dry season [ev_crop_yield_lott09_4]. In semi-arid Brazil, in a low-rainfall year, maize yielded very little whether or not it was grown among alley-cropped trees, with no significant difference between the two systems — the drought year erased the tree benefit rather than reversing it [ev_crop_yield_martins13_2]. A Senegal review finds no clear consensus on windbreak hedges in drought, with some studies reporting higher yields in drier years and others harm to rainfed crops [ev_drought_hazard_faosen24_17]. The understorey yield benefit holds in drought years only, since tree shade can lower understorey yields under normal rainfall, and the Kenyan household link to perceived drought held in Burat but not in Kinna [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_t3_drought_perception_quandt17_5]. Several findings are stand-ins or ratings rather than measurements: the Canadian and US findings are high-income evidence, and the FMNR finding is a practitioner rating [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The German soil-water difference was not significant everywhere and is high-income evidence, and the Nyando timber-sales finding is farmer-reported [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. The Honduran account is grey literature written by staff of the project that promoted the Quesungual system, so it may overstate the benefit; it does not say how severe the 1997 dry period was, and the trees come bundled with mulching, zero tillage, direct sowing and no burning, so the result cannot be credited to the trees alone [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2]. The parkland fodder statement is a review citation without a size [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. The Latin American silvopastoral findings are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume; the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year rather than with and without trees, and the Colombian forage result likely describes the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. The Ethiopian Faidherbia result is a drought-year comparison reported as an 'up to' figure; the same study reports its normal-season gain separately, so this hazard-year gain is not the usual yield effect [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. In shaded cocoa and coffee the evidence is split: a review cites that under warmer, water-limited conditions competition between trees and cacao for scarce soil water can reduce soil moisture and cacao yields below those of open-sun farms [ev_crop_yield_watts22_8]; and in the Ghana experiment the shade-by-drought interaction on yield was not significant, so shade did not prevent the drought-induced yield decline and only partly compensated for it [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]; the Ethiopian study did not directly observe benefits of diverse shade in the extreme climate shocks [ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]; and across cabruca cocoa farms in southern Bahia, Brazil, drought yield loss was unrelated to shade-tree ground cover [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2]. Apart from the Ghana field study, these harm findings are second-hand readings in reviews. The cocoa and coffee findings are crop-specific and enter because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop; the Ghana shade came from artificial shade nets rather than shade trees, so its transfer to agroforestry is borderline [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]. The Argentine multi-site study is the clearest statement of why severity matters: it explicitly frames the switch from facilitation to competition as a function of drought intensity, and shows the sign of the effect also depends on site aridity and on whether the stocking system is native-forest or planted silvopastoral, so it cannot be read as a single transferable number [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_2, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_3, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_4, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_5, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_6, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_1]. The French walnut-pea result is a cushioned loss, not an absolute gain: agroforestry pea yield remained below the full-sun yield in both rainfall regimes, and the smaller drought-specific loss is a relative measure against each system's own rainfed baseline, from a single season and site with the two conditions not randomised within the parcel [ev_crop_yield_blan22_2, ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3]. Both of these are upper-middle-income Argentina and high-income France, sitting at a different distance from the low- and lower-middle-income target than the Kenyan and Ethiopian evidence already in this row. A multi-species silvopasture trial on degraded rangeland in arid India adds a further measured harm result on the pastoral side: understorey herbage yield fell further under drought beneath every tree and shrub species than in the treeless control, which the authors attribute to shading and competition for soil moisture; the same trial measured the trees also supplying extra dry-season browse fodder, a trade-off kept separate here rather than netting off against the herbage loss [ev_drought_hazard_singhrao08_1, ev_forage_productivity_singhrao08_1, ev_forage_productivity_singhrao08_2]. This Indian evidence is lower-middle income, inside the low- and lower-middle-income target. In the Senegal shrub trial the soil next to the shrubs dried faster during the imposed drought than soil far from them in two of three subplots, even as the millet yield gain held; that trial is a single site and a single shrub species [ev_soil_moisture_bogie18_2, ev_crop_yield_bogie18_1].

Most findings say agroforestry reduces drought losses, but the result splits by type of agroforestry, and several measured results show no benefit or harm, especially in severe or extreme drought. On the benefit side: in Isiolo County communities in Kenya, households rated agroforestry important during drought, farmers said deep-rooted trees reach water from deep down and keep producing fruit when there is no rain, and 74% of respondents had planted trees with drought in mind; the study concludes that agroforestry can and does build livelihood resilience to drought, citing deep root systems that use a greater soil volume for water [ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_t3_drought_deeproots_quandt17_7, ev_t3_drought_farmerquote_quandt17_12, ev_t3_drought_intentional_quandt17_14, ev_t3_drought_conclusion_quandt17_10, ev_t3_drought_roots_quandt17_2, ev_t3_drought_lh_quandt17_1]. In a Senegal field trial, pearl millet grown among the native shrub Guiera senegalensis under an imposed in-season drought produced almost 10 times the biomass and over seven times more panicles than millet where the shrubs had been removed [ev_crop_yield_bogie18_1]. In an induced drought in eastern Canada only the monocrop lost yield, and the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Nyando District, Kenya, households in an agroforestry project typically used fewer detrimental coping strategies during hunger periods, and many farmers reported selling fuel wood and timber from their trees to buy food during the drought [ev_food_security_thorlak12_2, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. In a German alley-cropping system during a drought year, soil water content stayed lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system, though the differences were not significant at all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. In Sahelian parklands, trees make up a large share of high-quality livestock fodder, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, a practitioner article on the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system reports that, compared with farmers who remained with slash-and-burn, Quesungual farmers did not experience a total loss in maize production during the dry period of El Niño in 1997, which the authors put down to improved soil conditions [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2]. On paired on-farm plots in Ethiopia's Central Rift Valley, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns gave up to 85% more grain than open-field wheat in 2015, an El Niño year in which both yields were low [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. In Colombia, forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant in periods of intense drought while biomass in grass monoculture fell to 25% [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in 2009, the year with the lowest rainfall in several decades (440 mm), milk production still rose 10% on the previous year [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which reduces seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. Live fences of species such as Gliricidia sepium and Leucaena leucocephala supply livestock fodder in the dry season, when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. For shaded coffee and cocoa: in Ethiopia's Yayu coffee forest, the yield model for the climate-shock years found leguminous shade strongly raised coffee shrub yields at high canopy openness [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]; and reviews cite a 41% cut in evapotranspiration loss under coffee shade trees in the hot, dry season and low water stress in cacao grown with Gliricidia [ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_8, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11]. In a 25-year-old walnut-based alley-cropping system in southern France, winter pea still yielded less under the trees than in the full-sun control under both rainfall regimes, but the yield drop caused specifically by an imposed spring drought was smaller under the trees: full-sun yield fell 22% under drought while the alley-cropped yield rose by 12 to 20% relative to its own rainfed baseline, which the authors attribute to drought shifting yield formation from the shade-sensitive pod-set stage to grain filling [ev_crop_yield_blan22_2, ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3]. In a multi-site Argentine study of tree-covered pasture (silvopastoral systems) against treeless grassland, the normal-year forage benefit reversed under severe drought at some sites: at the semi-arid Santiago del Estero site the relative response swung from +2% in normal years to -89% in a dry year, while at the humid Chaco site it swung the other way, from -15% to +26%, and in the semi-arid aridity category overall there was no significant difference between systems in either normal or dry years — a result the authors attribute to tree-forage competition for water overtaking facilitation once drought intensity passes about 35% rainfall reduction [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_2, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_3, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_4, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_5, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_6].", "conditionality": "The rating is conflicting because the types of agroforestry disagree: trees and shrubs regenerated on cropland show a strong reduction in drought losses, general findings not tied to one type show a small one, and planted tree-crop alleys, shaded tree crops and silvopasture each have studies on both sides. Few of the benefit findings say how large the effect is. The clearest harm finding is a direct field measurement in Ghana: during the extreme drought of 2015/16 all cocoa plants under Albizia ferruginea shade trees died and cocoa under Antiaris toxicaria suffered 77% mortality, while cocoa in full sun kept higher sap flux and soil water content was higher in full sun, pointing to competition for water between shade trees and cocoa [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. What separates the sides is mainly system and severity: deep-rooted trees in dryland fields and fodder trees in pastures read as buffers, while in shaded tree crops under extreme drought the trees compete with the crop for scarce soil water. Trade-offs pull the other way, now with more direct field evidence: in a semi-arid Kenyan growing season that received only 317 mm of rain, maize under dispersed Grevillea robusta trees yielded 0.02 t/ha against 1.53 t/ha in unshaded sole maize, a near-total loss under the trees in a dry season [ev_crop_yield_lott09_4]. The understorey yield benefit holds in drought years only, since tree shade can lower understorey yields under normal rainfall, and the Kenyan household link to perceived drought held in Burat but not in Kinna [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_t3_drought_perception_quandt17_5]. Several findings are stand-ins or ratings rather than measurements: the Canadian and US findings are high-income evidence, and the FMNR finding is a practitioner rating [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The German soil-water difference was not significant everywhere and is high-income evidence, and the Nyando timber-sales finding is farmer-reported [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. The Honduran account is grey literature written by staff of the project that promoted the Quesungual system, so it may overstate the benefit; it does not say how severe the 1997 dry period was, and the trees come bundled with mulching, zero tillage, direct sowing and no burning, so the result cannot be credited to the trees alone [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2]. The Latin American silvopastoral findings are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume; the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year rather than with and without trees, and the Colombian forage result likely describes the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. Apart from the Ghana field study, these harm findings are second-hand readings in reviews. The cocoa and coffee findings are crop-specific and enter because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop; the Ghana shade came from artificial shade nets rather than shade trees, so its transfer to agroforestry is borderline [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]. A US silvopasture study lists better water infiltration among silvopasture's services, used here as a soil-water component of drought [ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9]. In a French walnut-based alley-cropping system, imposed spring drought cut full-sun pea yield by 22% while the alley-cropped yield rose 12 to 20% relative to its own rainfed baseline, though alley-cropped pea still yielded less overall than the full-sun control in both rainfall regimes [ev_crop_yield_blan22_2, ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3].

The French result adds a fourth high-income unit to this scope row: a single season and site, drought imposed experimentally with rainout shelters, and the two conditions not randomised within the parcel; the benefit is a smaller drought-specific loss, not a yield advantage over full sun [ev_crop_yield_blan22_2, ev_drought_hazard_blan22_3].

mitigation_mechanism: For trees and shrubs kept or regenerated on cropland, the evidence points to a strong reduction in drought losses. On paired on-farm plots in Ethiopia's Central Rift Valley, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns gave up to 85% more grain than open-field wheat in 2015, an El Niño year in which both yields were low [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. In a Senegal field trial, pearl millet grown among the native shrub Guiera senegalensis under an imposed in-season drought produced almost 10 times the biomass and over seven times more panicles than millet where the shrubs had been removed [ev_crop_yield_bogie18_1]. Hydraulic redistribution in Sahelian parklands lets crop roots use deep soil moisture reached only by tree roots [ev_soil_water_retention_vannoordwijk21_3]. The Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Sahelian parklands, tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, a practitioner article on the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system reports that Quesungual farmers did not experience a total loss in maize production during the dry period of El Niño in 1997, unlike farmers who kept slash-and-burn [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2].
caveats: One measured result runs the other way: in the same Senegal trial, soil next to the shrubs dried faster during the imposed drought than soil far from them or in crop-only plots in two of three subplots [ev_soil_moisture_bogie18_2]. The Senegal results come from a single site and one shrub species, and the Ethiopian result is a drought-year comparison reported as an 'up to' figure from one study [ev_crop_yield_bogie18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. The deep-water finding is a review citing earlier work and describes a part of drought impact rather than a measured loss [ev_soil_water_retention_vannoordwijk21_3]. The FMNR finding is a practitioner rating of a slight benefit, not a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts], and the parkland fodder statement is a review citation without a size [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. The Honduran account is grey literature written by staff of the project that promoted the system, does not say how severe the dry period was, and bundles the trees with mulching, zero tillage, direct sowing and no burning, so the result cannot be credited to the trees alone [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2].

mitigation_mechanism: Under drought, shade over cocoa and coffee has been found to protect the crop, to compete with it for water, and to make no difference. On the protective side, in Ethiopia's Yayu coffee forest the yield model for the climate-shock years found leguminous shade strongly raised coffee shrub yields at high canopy openness [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]; a review cites a 41% cut in evapotranspiration loss under coffee shade trees in the hot, dry season (Lin 2006) [ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_8]; and another cites low water stress in cacao grown with Gliricidia (Schwendenmann et al. 2010; Köhler et al. 2010) [ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11]. On the competing side, the strongest measurement is a Ghana field study of a cocoa plantation through the extreme 2015/16 El Niño drought: all cocoa plants under the shade tree Albizia ferruginea died, cocoa under Antiaris toxicaria suffered 77% mortality with sap flux density cut to 115 g cm2 day1 against 170 in full sun, sap-flux recovery afterwards was 163 in full sun against 37 under Antiaris, and soil water was higher in full sun, which the authors link to strong competition for soil water [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. A review adds that under warmer, water-limited conditions tree-cacao competition can push soil moisture and cacao yields below open-sun farms (Blaser et al. 2018) [ev_crop_yield_watts22_8]. Between them sit no-effect findings: in a Ghana rainwater-suppression experiment the shade-by-drought interaction on yield was not significant, so shade did not prevent the drought-induced yield decline [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]; the Ethiopian study did not directly observe benefits of diverse shade in the extreme climate shock [ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]; and across cabruca cocoa farms in southern Bahia, Brazil, drought yield loss was unrelated to shade-tree ground cover [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2].
caveats: Studies disagree, and what separates the sides, as far as the evidence says, is twofold. First, whether the shade trees draw on the same scarce soil water as the crop: the losses, including the Ghana die-off, are attributed to that competition [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1, ev_crop_yield_watts22_8], while the gains come with a named companion tree (Gliricidia) or a shade-management setting (canopy openness) [ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11, ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]. Shade-tree species, density and canopy management are therefore the design questions; in the Ghana study the outcome differed by shade-tree species, total loss under one and heavy loss under the other [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. Second, a higher yield under shade is not the same as protection from drought: the Ghana experiment found the better performance of cocoa under shade can only partly compensate for the reduced yield during drought episodes [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]. The Ghana experiment's shade came from artificial shade nets, not shade trees, so it has no below-ground competition and its transfer to agroforestry is borderline [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]. All units are crop-specific (cocoa or coffee) and enter because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop. The Ghana die-off was measured in an extreme drought; most other units do not say how severe the drought was [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]. The review units are second-hand readings of earlier studies, and only the evapotranspiration figure carries a size [ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_8, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11, ev_crop_yield_watts22_8]. The field units are from upper-middle-income Brazil, low-income Ethiopia and lower-middle-income Ghana; the review units record no country [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_morel24_1, ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2, ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1].

mitigation_mechanism: In silvopastoral systems, the benefit runs through fodder availability and herd condition during drought. In Colombia, forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant through intense drought while grass monoculture biomass fell to a quarter [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in the lowest-rainfall year in several decades milk production still rose 10% on the previous year [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which is said to reduce seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. A US silvopasture study lists better water infiltration among silvopasture's services, used here as a soil-water component of drought [ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9]. In a multi-site Argentine study, forage production under trees exceeded treeless grassland or pasture at drought intensities at or below the authors' dry-year threshold, and held up in very humid areas in both normal and dry years, a result corroborated by a companion reading of the same sites [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_3, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_1].
caveats: The evidence splits by drought severity and which forage layer is measured, rather than agreeing on one direction. On the benefit side, the Colombian and Argentine forage and milk gains above hold up to around the authors' dry-year threshold [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_3, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_1]. On the harm side, the same Argentine study found the benefit reverses under severe drought at some sites: at semi-arid Santiago del Estero the relative forage response swung from +2% in normal years to -89% in a dry year, at the humid Chaco site it swung the other way (-15% to +26%), and in the semi-arid aridity category overall there was no significant difference between systems in either normal or dry years — the authors attribute the reversal to tree-forage competition for water overtaking facilitation above about 35% rainfall reduction [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_2, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_4, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_5, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_6]. A multi-species silvopasture trial on degraded rangeland in arid India adds a second harm result: understorey herbage yield fell further under drought beneath every tree and shrub species than in the treeless control, attributed by the authors to shading and competition for soil moisture, though the same trees supplied extra dry-season browse fodder not counted in that herbage comparison [ev_drought_hazard_singhrao08_1, ev_forage_productivity_singhrao08_1, ev_forage_productivity_singhrao08_2]. What separates both sides is drought intensity and which forage layer is counted: below a site-specific dry-year threshold, or when browse is counted alongside grass, silvopasture holds or gains; once drought crosses that threshold, or when only understorey herbage is counted, tree-grass competition for scarce water dominates and the system does worse than open pasture. The Latin American silvopastoral units are mostly earlier studies cited in a Spanish-language review and a CATIE edited volume rather than new primary measurements; the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year rather than with and without trees, and the Colombian forage result likely describes the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. The clearest primary magnitudes (Argentina, Colombia, India) are upper-middle or lower-middle income, and the US unit is high income, so the row as a whole transfers only as adjacent [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_2, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9, ev_drought_hazard_singhrao08_1].

mitigation_mechanism: In mixed crop-livestock systems the 2 papers that name this system point the same way, a small reduction in drought impact without a stated size; this differs from the overall agroforestry drought row, where the studies disagree. In two Isiolo County communities in Kenya, households rated agroforestry important during drought, farmers said deep-rooted trees reach water from deep down and keep producing fruit when there is no rain, and 74% of respondents had planted trees with drought in mind; the study concludes that agroforestry can and does build livelihood resilience to drought, citing deep root systems that use a greater soil volume for water [ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_t3_drought_deeproots_quandt17_7, ev_t3_drought_farmerquote_quandt17_12, ev_t3_drought_intentional_quandt17_14, ev_t3_drought_conclusion_quandt17_10, ev_t3_drought_roots_quandt17_2, ev_t3_drought_lh_quandt17_1]. In Nyando District, Kenya, households in an agroforestry project typically used fewer detrimental coping strategies during hunger periods, and many farmers reported selling fuel wood and timber from their trees to buy food during the drought [ev_food_security_thorlak12_2, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1].
caveats: Both papers are from Kenya and rest on household surveys and farmer interviews, not on measured drought losses with and without trees. In Isiolo the link between agroforestry and perceived drought held in Burat but not in Kinna [ev_t3_drought_perception_quandt17_5]. The Nyando findings use coping strategies and tree-product sales as stand-ins for drought impact, and the timber sales are farmer-reported [ev_food_security_thorlak12_2, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. No finding says how large the benefit is, and none measures it in a severe or extreme drought.

mitigation_mechanism: Shade trees cool the understorey crop in shaded perennial systems. In cocoa agroforestry, canopy shade provides a more stable microclimate, with lower and more buffered maximum and minimum temperatures than in monoculture [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1]. A synthesis of empirical co-benefits found shade trees reduce canopy temperatures by 2 to 4 degrees Celsius, mitigating heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4], and a shaded coffee plot in Costa Rica measured a 1.7 degree Celsius reduction in maximum air temperature compared with full sun [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4]. A West African cocoa study notes, citing earlier work, that cocoa agroforestry with well-managed shade lowers air and soil temperature extremes [ev_microclimate_buffering_arizasal23_1].
caveats: This evidence base is limited to shaded perennial-crop systems (cocoa and coffee) and does not cover severe or extreme heat events: none of the cited sources measures mitigation under an intense heat episode, so the cooling shown here is a moderate-weather finding, not a tested defence against a heatwave. The cocoa statement is second-hand and gives no size [ev_microclimate_buffering_arizasal23_1].

mitigation_mechanism: Silvopastoral systems cut heat stress in cattle: intensive shrub–tree–rotational pasture models in the dry Colombian Caribbean reduce it, and eucalyptus–brachiaria systems in Brazil reduced the area at critical animal thermal-comfort levels by 20 to 100% against monoculture pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. Tree shade in pastures is associated with 13 to 28% increases in milk production and weight gain [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4]. Under tree crowns, temperature reductions of 2 to 9 °C relative to open areas have been reported, and in Cañas, Costa Rica, temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. mitigation_mechanism: The evidence points to a moderate reduction in waterlogging losses: trees take excess water out of waterlogged soil. A review reports, second-hand, that under waterlogging in Punjab, India, agroforestry systems had higher evapotranspiration than sole crops, indicating greater removal of excess water from the soil and a better soil environment for plant growth [ev_waterlogging_hazard_dobhal24_9]. mitigation_mechanism: Windbreaks and shelterbelts work mechanically, by slowing the wind reaching the sheltered crop. A review on windbreak airflow states that a major effect of a windbreak is to reduce the incidence of low-frequency, high-magnitude damage events such as sandblasting or lodging [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_cleugh98_3]. The zone of reduced wind speed behind a windbreak typically extends 10 to 20 tree heights downwind, so large fields often need multiple barriers [ev_windbreak_protection_dobhal24_15]. In China, farmland shelterbelts cut wind speed by 35.8% compared with unsheltered farmland [ev_windbreak_protection_hao26_1]. In Senegal, windbreak hedges are described as having a major impact on wind and playing an important role in protecting sandy, degraded soils from wind erosion [ev_windbreak_protection_faosen24_12]. In India, live fences are used as windbreaks and to raise soil-moisture retention through litter accumulation [ev_windbreak_protection_moran18_4]. More generally, on-farm trees serving as windbreaks and shelterbelts are also used to supply material for rebuilding storm-damaged property [ev_windbreak_protection_lasco14_1]. In Mexican shaded coffee, vegetation management had a significant effect on landslide risk but not on coffee harvest lost [ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6]. In Puerto Rico after Hurricane Maria, coffee patches under shade trees were on some farms not as severely damaged as patches in open sun [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_perfecto19_4].
caveats: Against this, a Spanish-language climate-risk review lists an explicit maladaptation example: planting shade trees that increases storm vulnerability by damaging existing infrastructure when the trees come down in high winds [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5]. The Puerto Rico study makes the same point for coffee: when winds are very strong, large shade trees are toppled and their trunks and canopies do considerable damage to the coffee below [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_perfecto19_5]. The overall rating is conflicting because the types of agroforestry disagree: windbreak and boundary-planting evidence reads as a benefit, while shaded tree crops are themselves split, between shelter and falling-tree damage in Puerto Rico and a Mexican coffee study that found no relationship between management and harvest loss [ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6]. Only the Chinese shelterbelt study states a size for the wind-speed reduction; the rest describe mechanism or role without a size. Apart from the Puerto Rico hurricane, the evidence covers routine wind and erosion control rather than storm damage, and the Puerto Rico observations are qualitative and from a high-income country [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_perfecto19_4, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_perfecto19_5]. The Chinese and Mexican findings are from upper-middle-income countries and the Senegalese and Indian ones from lower-middle-income countries.

mitigation_mechanism: Drought severely damages agroforestry itself: it kills the trees of the system and cuts its output. Severe drought can raise tree seedling mortality by 35 to 40% because seedlings cannot match transpiration demands [ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_3]. In Colombia, droughts provoked by El Niño between 2015 and 2016 caused significant losses of trees planted by the project, and the area under the most recently planted intensive silvopastoral systems fell by 45 percent in the severe 2019 drought in a survey of 285 farms [ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_5, ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_4]. In cabruca cocoa agroforests in southern Bahia, Brazil, cocoa tree mortality was 15% during the El Niño event against under 1% normally, 7% of the 317 woody shade trees died, and potential yield fell from 242 to 26 kg/ha, an 89% reduction, still 83% lower nine months after the drought ended [ev_establishment_survival_gateau18_1, ev_establishment_survival_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_gateau18_1]. A tropics review also cites a study in which drought cut the stem diameter of one large tree species, Saurauia nudiflora, by 80% against a 5% decrease in the smaller Archidendron bubalinum [ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_7].
caveats: This is an establishment-phase risk first, which is the phase a project funds and is exposed to: the measured damage falls mostly on seedlings and newly planted trees [ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_3, ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_5], though established cabruca cocoa and its shade trees also died in the El Niño drought [ev_establishment_survival_gateau18_1, ev_establishment_survival_gateau18_2]. Seedling and young-system losses dominate: the Colombian source notes established systems were more drought-resilient than traditional pastures while young ones are vulnerable in their initial years [ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_4], and one cited study found drought did not increase seedling mortality, though growth was impaired [ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_4]. The Bahia cocoa losses carry no unshaded comparator, so they show the damage to the asset, not whether shade made it worse or better [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_1]. The cocoa findings are about one crop and count because shaded tree-crop systems are judged on their host crop. Brazil and Colombia are upper-middle income, close to but outside the low- and lower-middle-income countries this tool targets [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_1, ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_4]. The stem-diameter finding is second-hand, names two tree species and shows that large trees can be hit far harder than small ones [ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_7].

mitigation_mechanism: Strong wind and storms moderately damage agroforestry itself, mainly its trees. On 28 coffee farms in Puerto Rico, Hurricane Maria stripped an average 37.5% of the shade canopy, from about 40% cover to about 25% [ev_climate_shock_perfecto19_1], and farms with denser shade before the storm lost no smaller share of their canopy [ev_climate_shock_perfecto19_2]. All the interviewed farmers who had shade trees reported significant damage to them, and projected harvest fell to 219 kg/ha against a normal of about 1272 kg/ha [ev_climate_shock_perfecto19_3]. A study cited by Philpott et al., comparing abandoned pastures, mixed plantations, abandoned cacao and forests, found that areas with more complex vegetation were least resistant to hurricane damage, losing larger and more trees [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_philpott08_8]. In a shaded-coffee trial in Paraná, Brazil, the Mimosa scabrella shade trees showed poor resistance to wind, breaking under gusts above 15 m/s [ev_climate_shock_caramori96_3]. In the establishment phase, silvopastoral tree seedlings need protection from excess sun and wind, among other threats [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_diasf08_4]. The compiler of the Burkina Faso WOCAT sheet on assisted natural regeneration of degraded land judged the technology to cope well with local windstorm [ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1358_2017_local_windstorm].
caveats: The findings only partly agree. Against the damage findings, a field study in shaded coffee in Chiapas, Mexico, found minimal vegetation damage from a hurricane whose winds the study records as mild [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_philpott08_7], and a coconut review from Kerala, India, reports second-hand that the coconut palm withstands typhoons [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_kumar22_1]. The hurricane-damage result is second-hand, compares abandoned land uses and forests rather than managed agroforestry, and names no location [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_philpott08_8]. The Brazilian wind-breakage finding is about one shade-tree species at a single research farm [ev_climate_shock_caramori96_3]. The seedling finding lists wind among several establishment needs alongside trampling, grazing, weeds and fire [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_diasf08_4], and the Burkina Faso rating is a practitioner judgement, not a measurement [ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1358_2017_local_windstorm]. Burkina Faso is low income, India lower-middle and Brazil and Mexico upper-middle income. The Puerto Rico results come from one very strong hurricane in a high-income country; the authors suggest the storm may have been so strong that tree windbreaks were ineffective, and the harvest loss covers the whole farm, berries and coffee bushes included, not only the shade trees [ev_climate_shock_perfecto19_1, ev_climate_shock_perfecto19_3].
